terms.def: A yearly programme of tests that verifies a DP vessel's redundancy concept still performs as documented in its FMEA. Trials typically simulate worst-case failures — thruster loss, power section blackout, reference dropout — and confirm the vessel maintains position within its post-failure capability. Findings feed back into the FMEA and the vessel's DP operations manuals.

A decision-support matrix that defines the operational, environmental and equipment limits for a specific DP activity, and the actions required as conditions move from normal (green) through advisory (blue/yellow) to emergency (red). The ASOG turns the vessel's FMEA and capability analysis into clear go/no-go criteria the bridge team can act on in real time.

A propulsion unit that can rotate through 360 degrees, producing thrust in any horizontal direction without a conventional rudder. Azimuth thrusters give DP vessels the omnidirectional force needed for precise station keeping and are a key input to thruster allocation logic.

A total loss of electrical power on the main switchboard, leaving the vessel without propulsion and station-keeping ability. Preventing blackout — and proving that a single failure cannot cause one — is central to DP class 2 and 3 design, power management strategy and FMEA analysis. Blackout recovery time is a critical performance measure tested during trials.

A transverse propulsion unit mounted in a tunnel near the bow, used to push the fore end of the vessel sideways. Bow thrusters support berthing, low-speed manoeuvring and DP station keeping, where they typically provide the forward lateral force in the thruster allocation scheme.

terms.term: CAMO — Critical Activity Mode of Operation
terms.def: The vessel configuration — power plant, thrusters, control systems and reference systems — that delivers the highest practical level of redundancy for safety-critical DP activities. Operating in CAMO means a single failure should not exceed the worst-case failure design intent, keeping the vessel within its post-failure capability.

A polar diagram showing the maximum environmental conditions (wind, current, waves) in which a DP vessel can hold position, plotted for every heading. Capability plots are produced for intact condition and for defined failure cases, and are used in operational planning to confirm adequate margin before starting work.

Running a DP vessel's power plant with the bus-tie breakers between switchboard sections closed, so all generators feed a common bus. Closed bus improves fuel efficiency and reduces running hours, but requires demonstrably fast, reliable protection systems so that a single fault cannot propagate across the whole plant — a major focus of modern FMEA and HIL testing.

A single event or hidden dependency that defeats supposedly independent redundant systems at the same time — for example contaminated fuel affecting all generators, or a shared cooling line serving both switchboard rooms. Hunting down common-mode failures is one of the primary objectives of a DP FMEA.

A continuous online function in the DP control system that predicts whether the vessel could still hold position and heading if the worst-case single failure occurred right now, given current weather and thruster loading. If the prediction fails, the system raises an alarm so the crew can reduce exposure before a failure actually happens. Required for DP class 2 and 3 vessels.

Satellite positioning enhanced by correction data from reference stations, improving accuracy from metres to decimetres. DGNSS is the workhorse position reference for most DP operations, usually operated in pairs from independent providers and cross-checked against a different reference technology such as hydroacoustics or laser.

The standardised three-level status indication for DP operations: green (normal), yellow (degraded — prepare to suspend work), and red (emergency — terminate work and move to safe position). Alert levels are broadcast to relevant stations such as the drill floor, dive control or crane cab so everyone reacts consistently to a change in DP status.

The IMO equipment classes defining a DP vessel's tolerance to failure. DP 1 has no redundancy; DP 2 must withstand any single failure of an active component without losing position; DP 3 must additionally survive loss of an entire compartment to fire or flooding, with physically separated redundant systems. The required class is set by the consequence of losing position for the activity performed.

The observed excursion pattern of a vessel about its setpoint while holding station — effectively a scatter plot of position error over time. Footprint plots recorded during trials and operations give a practical measure of station-keeping performance in the prevailing conditions.

Any undesired event affecting DP integrity — from a single reference rejection to a full drive-off or drift-off. Industry schemes such as IMCA's station-keeping incident reporting collect and anonymise these events so lessons propagate across the fleet; investigating and learning from them is a recognised part of DP assurance.

A computer-controlled system that automatically holds a vessel's position and heading using its own thrusters, based on continuous input from position reference systems, gyrocompasses, motion sensors and wind sensors. DP enables offshore drilling, diving, construction, cable lay and shuttle offloading without anchors, and is the core discipline behind Maritime.Studio's consulting and training services.

The certified officer who operates the DP system on the bridge, monitors position references, power and thrusters, and executes the ASOG when conditions change. DPO qualification follows a structured path of induction and simulator courses, logged seatime and assessment — most commonly under the Nautical Institute scheme.

A loss of position in which the vessel is carried off station by wind, waves and current because it no longer has enough thrust — typically after power or thruster failures. Drift-off is the "passive" loss-of-position mode, in contrast to drive-off, and the post-failure capability analysis exists to predict and prevent it.

A loss of position in which the DP system actively powers the vessel away from its setpoint — usually caused by a faulty position reference, sensor error or control system malfunction that the system acts upon. Drive-offs develop fast and are a key scenario in DPO emergency training and simulator drills.

The combination of wind, wave and current limits within which a vessel can safely conduct a given DP operation, derived from capability plots and operational experience. Working inside the envelope preserves margin for the worst-case failure; the ASOG defines what to do as conditions approach its edge.

A DNV notation expressing, as a set of percentile figures, a vessel's ability to keep position in Norwegian continental shelf weather conditions under defined failure states. ERN offers a compact comparative measure of station-keeping robustness between vessels.

The practical sea trials that validate the FMEA's conclusions by deliberately injecting failures — tripping breakers, failing thrusters, disconnecting references — and observing whether the system responds as the analysis predicted. Discrepancies between predicted and observed behaviour are among the most valuable findings in DP verification.

terms.term: FMEA — Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
terms.def: A systematic engineering study that examines every component of a DP vessel's power, propulsion and control systems, asks how each can fail, and traces the effect of each failure on station keeping. The FMEA defines the vessel's worst-case failure design intent and proves — on paper and then in proving trials — that no single failure exceeds it. It is the foundational document of DP assurance, and a core specialty of Maritime.Studio's consulting practice.

The umbrella term for satellite constellations — GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou — that provide worldwide positioning. In DP, raw GNSS is refined with differential corrections (DGNSS) and monitored closely, because satellite signal anomalies are a classic trigger for reference rejection or drive-off scenarios.

A north-seeking compass that uses a fast-spinning rotor (or fibre-optic/ring-laser equivalent) to find true north independent of the Earth's magnetic field. DP vessels carry two or three gyrocompasses, since heading is as critical to station keeping as position — a heading error rotates every other measurement.

Testing a real DP control system or power management system against a real-time simulation of the vessel, so that failure scenarios too risky or impractical to create on board — sensor freezes, network storms, protection race conditions — can be exercised systematically. HIL complements FMEA proving trials by covering software behaviour that hardware trials cannot safely reach.

The DP function that automatically maintains the vessel's heading against environmental forces, usually while position is also controlled. Choosing the optimal heading — typically weathervaning into the dominant environment — minimises thruster load and preserves capability margin.

A position reference that measures range and bearing to transponders deployed on the seabed using acoustic signals — in ultra-short, short or long baseline configurations. HPR is independent of satellites, making it a valuable complement to DGNSS, particularly for deepwater drilling and subsea construction.

A back-up manual control system, separate from the main DP controllers, that lets the operator command combined thruster output with a single joystick if the DP system fails. It provides a simple, robust fallback layer between full automatic DP and individual manual thruster levers.

A semi-automatic DP operating mode in which the operator commands vessel movement with a joystick while the system coordinates the thrusters — often with automatic heading control engaged. Joystick mode is used for close manoeuvring, approach phases and DPO training in vessel handling.

A relative position reference that measures range and bearing to reflective targets mounted on a nearby structure — a platform, rig or another vessel — using a rotating laser. Because it positions the vessel relative to the asset it is working beside rather than in absolute coordinates, it is the reference of choice for close-proximity DP operations such as platform supply and walk-to-work.

An inertial sensor measuring the vessel's roll, pitch and heave. The DP system uses MRU data to correct position references for lever-arm and attitude effects — an antenna at the masthead swings metres as the ship rolls — making accurate motion data essential to stable position keeping.

Running the power plant with bus-tie breakers open, splitting the switchboard into independent islands each feeding its own thrusters. Open bus provides robust physical fault separation — a fault on one island cannot black out the other — at the cost of higher fuel consumption and generator running hours compared with closed bus.

The temporary loss or rejection of a position reference signal — from satellite shading, acoustic interference, target obstruction or sensor fault. The DP system rides through short dropouts on its mathematical model, but sustained loss of references degrades position estimation and triggers escalation per the ASOG.

Any sensor system that tells the DP system where the vessel is: DGNSS, hydroacoustics, taut wire, laser and radar-based systems. DP class 2 and 3 operations require at least three references based on at least two different measurement principles, so that a common failure cannot silently corrupt the position solution.

The control system that supervises the vessel's power plant — starting and stopping generators, balancing load, shedding non-essential consumers and preventing blackout. In DP vessels the PMS and DP system work in close coordination, and PMS failure modes are examined line by line in the FMEA.

The provision of independent, duplicated systems so that a single failure does not stop the vessel keeping position. True redundancy requires more than duplication: the redundant groups must be genuinely independent — separate power, cooling, control and (for DP 3) physical compartments — which is exactly what the FMEA sets out to prove.

The planned relocation of a drilling rig between well locations, involving anchor handling vessels, tow masters and detailed procedures. For moored rigs it is a major marine operation with its own risk assessments and weather criteria; DP units instead transit under their own station-keeping capability.

Two or more independent activities conducted at the same time and place — for example diving while crane operations proceed, or a PSV alongside during helicopter operations. SIMOPS require a combined risk assessment and a clear hierarchy of control, because the safe limits for one activity can conflict with another's.

Any single component, system or event whose failure alone would cause loss of position — the thing a redundant DP vessel must not have. Identifying and eliminating (or at least documenting) single-point failures is the central purpose of the FMEA and the redundancy design it verifies.

Maintaining a vessel's position and heading within defined limits against wind, waves and current — by anchors and mooring, by dynamic positioning, or by a combination. Station-keeping integrity is the fundamental deliverable of every DP system, and the loss of it defines a DP incident.

A vessel configuration selected for lower-consequence DP activities, where the full redundancy of CAMO is not required and some efficiency or operational flexibility is gained in exchange for accepted, documented risk. The choice between CAMO and TAM — and who may authorise it — is defined in the vessel's DP operations documentation.

A mechanical position reference that lowers a weight to the seabed and measures the angle and length of the constantly tensioned wire to compute relative position. Simple and independent of both satellites and acoustics, taut wire remains a trusted third-principle reference in shallow to medium water depths.

The algorithm inside the DP controller that translates the required total force and turning moment into individual commands for each thruster — respecting thruster limits, forbidden zones and failure states while minimising power consumption. Allocation behaviour after a thruster failure is a key subject of FMEA analysis and trials.

Battery-backed power supplies that keep DP controllers, reference systems and critical instrumentation alive through transients and blackouts. DP rules require redundant, segregated UPS arrangements, and UPS battery condition and changeover behaviour are standard items in annual DP trials.

The defined radius (or radii) around the vessel's setpoint used to grade position excursions — typically an inner alert circle and outer action circles tied to yellow and red DP alert states. Watch circle sizes are set per operation, based on the consequence of excursion and the physical constraints of the task.

A forecast period during which environmental conditions are expected to stay within the limits required for a planned marine operation, including contingency time to reach a safe state if the forecast deteriorates. Marine operations standards require defined operational criteria and forecast reliability margins before committing to weather-restricted work.

Sensors measuring relative wind speed and direction, which the DP system uses for wind feed-forward — countering gusts with thrust before the vessel is pushed off position. Because a faulty wind sensor can command a real thrust response, wind sensor failure modes feature prominently in DP incident statistics and FMEA studies.

The single failure with the greatest impact on station-keeping capability that the vessel is designed to withstand — for example loss of one complete switchboard section with its thrusters. The WCFDI is defined during design, verified by the FMEA and trials, and underpins the consequence analysis running continuously during operations.

terms.def: The collective term for marine fuels that reduce greenhouse gas and pollutant emissions compared with conventional heavy fuel oil and marine gas oil — principally LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen and biofuels. Fuel choice now shapes newbuild design, crew training and compliance strategy, driven by the IMO GHG framework, EU regulation and charterer demand for green tonnage.

A zero-carbon fuel candidate that burns without emitting CO₂ and can be produced from renewable electricity ("green ammonia"). Its challenges are toxicity — even low concentrations are hazardous to crew — lower energy density than oil fuels, and the need for pilot fuel and NOₓ/N₂O control in engines. First ammonia dual-fuel engines and bunkering pilots are moving the concept from research into early commercial service, with dedicated crew safety training a prerequisite.

Design and operational measures that manage the acute toxicity of ammonia when it is carried or burned as a marine fuel. Because NH₃ is harmful to humans at low airborne concentrations, ammonia-fuelled ship designs define hazardous and toxic zones around tanks, vent masts, bunker stations and fuel preparation rooms, supported by gas detection, water spray systems, double-walled piping and dedicated ventilation. Crew procedures, personal protective equipment and emergency response planning for ammonia release are central to class and flag approval of these vessels.

Propulsion arrangements that use lithium-ion battery systems either as the sole energy source (fully electric) or in combination with combustion engines (hybrid). Batteries allow zero-emission operation on short routes and in port, enable peak shaving and spinning reserve on hybrid vessels, and can improve fuel efficiency of diesel-electric plants by letting engines run at optimal load. Norway's ferry sector has been an early large-scale adopter, and battery systems are increasingly combined with alternative fuels on offshore and coastal tonnage.

Liquefied biomethane produced from organic waste streams such as manure, sewage or food waste, upgraded to natural gas quality and liquefied for use in LNG-fuelled ships. Chemically it is interchangeable with fossil LNG, so existing LNG engines, tanks and bunkering infrastructure can use it without modification. On a well-to-wake basis its greenhouse gas footprint can be far lower than fossil LNG, which makes it a practical compliance option under frameworks such as FuelEU Maritime, though available volumes are currently limited.

Drop-in fuels produced from biological feedstocks — most commonly FAME biodiesel and HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil) — blended with or replacing conventional marine fuels. Their appeal is that existing engines and bunkering infrastructure can largely be used unchanged, making biofuel blends the fastest route to near-term greenhouse gas reductions while sustainability of feedstock and certification (well-to-wake accounting) remain the key questions.

The vapour continuously generated as cryogenic LNG (stored at about −162 °C) absorbs heat through tank insulation. Ships manage BOG by burning it in the engines, re-liquefying it, or — as a last resort — controlled venting via the gas combustion unit. BOG management is central to LNG fuel system design and to the gas-related training required under the IGF Code.

The mandatory document issued to a ship on delivery of fuel, recording quantity, density, sulphur content and supplier details as required by MARPOL Annex VI. BDNs and the associated fuel samples must be retained on board for inspection and form the primary evidence that bunkered fuel complies with sulphur limits. As alternative fuels enter service, BDN information is also increasingly used to document fuel origin and emission factors for regimes such as the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime.

Taking fuel on board — historically a routine oil transfer, now increasingly a specialised operation as LNG, methanol and ammonia enter service. Alternative-fuel bunkering introduces cryogenic or toxic transfer hazards, simultaneous-operations (SIMOPS) restrictions, dedicated safety zones and crew competence requirements, governed by standards such as the IGF Code and port-specific LNG bunkering rules.

The IMO's operational carbon-efficiency measure, rating ships annually from A to E based on CO₂ emitted per cargo capacity and distance sailed. Ships rated D for three consecutive years or E in any year must file a corrective action plan, making CII a direct commercial driver for slow steaming, hull and propeller optimisation, hybridisation and fuel switching.

Storage of fuels in liquefied form at very low temperatures, such as LNG at about −162 °C or liquid hydrogen at about −253 °C, to achieve a practical energy volume on board. Cryogenic tanks use heavy insulation and cold-resistant materials like stainless steel or nickel alloys, since ordinary carbon steel becomes brittle at these temperatures. Heat ingress inevitably vaporises some liquid as boil-off gas, so tank design, pressure control and gas management systems must be engineered together.

A fuel that can replace a conventional marine fuel in existing engines, tanks and bunkering infrastructure without hardware modification. Examples include certain biodiesel blends (FAME), hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) and bio-LNG used in place of fossil LNG. Drop-in fuels let operators cut well-to-wake emissions on today's fleet, which is valuable because most ships trading in 2050 will have been built with conventional machinery.

An engine that can run on a gaseous or low-flashpoint fuel — LNG, methanol or ammonia — ignited by a small quantity of conventional pilot fuel, and switch back to pure diesel operation when needed. Dual-fuel technology de-risks the transition to alternative fuels by preserving full capability on conventional fuel wherever the new fuel is unavailable.

Synthetic fuels, also called electrofuels or power-to-X fuels, produced from hydrogen made by electrolysis using renewable electricity, often combined with captured CO₂ or nitrogen. Marine-relevant examples include e-methanol, e-ammonia, e-methane and e-diesel. Their climate benefit depends entirely on the electricity source and, for carbon-containing e-fuels, on where the carbon comes from; they are widely seen as necessary for deep-sea decarbonisation but remain expensive and supply-constrained.

terms.term: EEDI / EEXI — Energy Efficiency Design & Existing Ship Index
terms.def: The IMO's technical energy-efficiency benchmarks: EEDI sets a minimum design efficiency for newbuilds, while EEXI applies an equivalent one-time requirement to existing ships. Together with the operational CII rating, they form the regulatory efficiency framework pushing engine power limitation, hull optimisation and alternative fuels across the world fleet.

A sea area designated under MARPOL Annex VI where stricter limits on emissions of sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides or both apply. In sulphur ECAs the fuel sulphur limit is 0.10%, compared with the 0.50% global cap, while NOx ECAs require Tier III engines on newer ships. Established ECAs include the Baltic Sea, the North Sea and the North American coasts, and the network continues to expand, directly shaping fuel choice and abatement strategies on affected trades.

The amount of energy a fuel contains per unit of mass (gravimetric) or volume (volumetric), a decisive factor in ship design and range. Conventional fuel oils are hard to beat: methanol carries roughly half the energy per volume of diesel oil, liquefied hydrogen roughly a quarter, and ammonia sits in between, before accounting for tank insulation and safety spacing. Lower energy density means larger tanks, lost cargo space or more frequent bunkering, which is why fuel choice is always weighed against a vessel's trading pattern.

The extension of the European Union Emissions Trading System to shipping, which took effect in 2024. Companies must surrender emission allowances for CO₂ from voyages between EU/EEA ports and half of the emissions on voyages into or out of the EU/EEA, phased in at 40% of 2024 emissions, 70% for 2025 and 100% from 2026. The scheme puts a direct price on carbon for ships above 5,000 GT and strengthens the business case for efficiency measures and lower-carbon fuels on European trades.

Equipment that washes sulphur oxides out of engine exhaust, allowing a ship to burn cheaper high-sulphur fuel while complying with the MARPOL global sulphur cap. Scrubbers come in open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid configurations; open-loop washwater discharge is banned in a growing list of ports and coastal states, keeping the technology's long-term role under debate.

The lowest temperature at which a fuel gives off enough vapour to ignite in air when exposed to an ignition source. SOLAS generally requires marine fuel oils to have a flashpoint above 60 °C, which conventional distillates and residual fuels meet. Fuels below that threshold, such as LNG, methanol and hydrogen, are classed as low-flashpoint fuels and may only be used under the additional safety arrangements of the IGF Code.

A device that converts fuel — typically hydrogen, or methanol/ammonia via reforming — directly into electricity through an electrochemical reaction, with no combustion and, for hydrogen, only water as exhaust. PEM fuel cells paired with batteries already power short-sea ferries and are being scaled toward offshore and coastal vessels, bringing new class rules and crew competence requirements with them.

The system that conditions and delivers gaseous or low-flashpoint fuel from the storage tanks to the consumers on a gas-fuelled ship. It typically includes pumps or pressure build-up units, vaporisers, heaters, filters and a gas valve unit that controls pressure and temperature to the engine's specification. The FGSS also incorporates safety functions such as double-walled piping, automatic shutdown and inerting connections, and its operation is a core element of IGF Code training for crews.

The EU regulation, applying from 2025, that caps the yearly average greenhouse gas intensity of energy used by ships calling at EU ports, with limits tightening in steps to 2050. Measured well-to-wake, it rewards alternative fuels and shore power (mandatory for containerships and cruise ships in major EU ports from 2030), and allows pooling of compliance across fleets — making fuel strategy a commercial optimisation problem, not just a technical one.

A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere relative to CO₂ over a chosen time horizon, usually 100 years (GWP100) or 20 years (GWP20). Methane's GWP is roughly 28–30 over 100 years but around 80 over 20 years, which is why methane slip from LNG engines attracts so much scrutiny. GWP values are used to convert different emissions into CO₂-equivalents so that fuels and technologies can be compared on a common basis.

Colour labels describing how hydrogen is produced, and by extension its climate footprint. Grey hydrogen is made from natural gas by steam reforming with the CO₂ released to the atmosphere; blue hydrogen uses the same process but captures and stores most of the CO₂; green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis powered by renewable electricity. The same labels carry over to derived fuels such as ammonia and methanol, and they matter because a ship burning grey-hydrogen-based fuel achieves little or no well-to-wake emission reduction.

A specific trade route — for example between two committed ports — where governments, ports, fuel suppliers and shipowners coordinate to make zero- or near-zero-emission shipping viable ahead of the global fleet. Corridors concentrate fuel availability, bunkering infrastructure, regulation and cargo demand in one place, acting as proving grounds for ammonia, methanol and hydrogen operations.

Residual fuel oil from the refining process, the traditional workhorse fuel of deep-sea shipping thanks to its low cost and high energy density. It is viscous and must be heated for storage and injection, and its high sulphur content means that since the IMO 2020 sulphur cap it may only be burned in ships fitted with exhaust gas cleaning systems. HFO serves as the emissions and cost baseline against which alternative fuels are usually compared.

The use of hydrogen (H₂) in fuel cells or internal combustion engines on board ships, producing no CO₂ at the point of use. Hydrogen is stored either compressed at high pressure or liquefied at about −253 °C, and its very low volumetric energy density currently limits it to short-sea applications such as ferries and offshore support vessels. It is a low-flashpoint fuel with a wide flammability range, so vessels using it fall under the IGF Code and require careful ventilation, gas detection and materials design; its climate benefit depends on whether the hydrogen is green, blue or grey.

A degradation mechanism in which hydrogen atoms diffuse into metals and reduce their ductility, making components prone to cracking under stress. It particularly affects high-strength steels used in tanks, piping, valves and fittings exposed to hydrogen, especially at high pressure. Designers of hydrogen-fuelled vessels mitigate it through material selection, such as suitable austenitic stainless steels, along with qualified welding procedures and inspection regimes.

The International Code of Safety for Ships Using Gases or Other Low-Flashpoint Fuels, mandatory under SOLAS for vessels fuelled by gases or other low-flashpoint fuels such as LNG. It sets goal-based requirements for fuel containment, bunkering arrangements, machinery spaces, ventilation, gas detection and hazardous area classification. Crews on IGF ships must complete STCW basic or advanced IGF Code training depending on their duties, and fuels not yet covered in detail, such as ammonia and hydrogen, are approved through the code's alternative design route pending dedicated provisions.

The IMO's mandatory scheme under MARPOL Annex VI requiring ships of 5,000 GT and above to record and report annual fuel oil consumption, distance travelled and hours underway to their flag State. The verified data feeds an IMO database and underpins the calculation of each ship's Carbon Intensity Indicator rating. It operates alongside, but separately from, the EU's MRV regulation, so many ships report under both systems.

The International Maritime Organization's roadmap for decarbonising shipping. The 2023 Revised GHG Strategy targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040 and a goal of at least 5% zero or near-zero emission fuel uptake by 2030. To deliver it, the IMO developed the Net-Zero Framework, combining a global fuel intensity standard with a GHG pricing mechanism; it was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, but formal adoption was postponed at an extraordinary session in October 2025 and negotiations continue in 2026, so it is not yet in force.

Procedures that replace air or fuel vapour in tanks and piping with an inert gas, usually nitrogen, so that a flammable mixture cannot form. On gas-fuelled ships, fuel lines and bunkering connections are purged with nitrogen before and after transfer, and tanks are inerted before gassing-up or before entry for maintenance. Correct inerting practice is a core safety barrier under the IGF Code, and the displaced atmosphere also creates asphyxiation hazards that crews must manage.

Liquefied natural gas, mainly methane cooled to about −162 °C, used as ship fuel in dual-fuel or pure gas engines. It is the most mature alternative fuel, with an established bunkering network and a large orderbook, and it virtually eliminates sulphur oxide and particulate emissions while cutting CO₂ at the funnel by roughly 20% compared with fuel oil. Its overall climate benefit is reduced by methane slip and upstream emissions, but LNG-fuelled ships can transition to bio-LNG or e-methane without engine changes.

Any fuel with a flashpoint below the 60 °C threshold that SOLAS sets for conventional marine fuel oils. The category covers LNG, methanol, hydrogen, LPG and ethane, all of which form ignitable vapours at normal ambient temperatures. Ships burning such fuels must comply with the IGF Code, which imposes additional requirements on tank location, ventilation, gas detection and crew certification compared with a conventional oil-fuelled vessel.

A distillate marine fuel similar to diesel, with low viscosity and typically very low sulphur content, used without heating. MGO is the standard fuel for many smaller vessels and for operation in Emission Control Areas where the 0.10% sulphur limit applies, and it commonly serves as pilot fuel in dual-fuel engines. It is cleaner-burning but more expensive than residual fuels, and it remains a fossil fuel with a corresponding CO₂ footprint.

A fuel or cargo containment system in which a thin metallic membrane, supported by insulation resting on the ship's inner hull, holds cryogenic liquid such as LNG. Membrane tanks use the hull shape efficiently and suit large volumes, which is why they dominate on LNG carriers and appear on large LNG-fuelled ships such as container vessels. They operate at near-atmospheric pressure, so boil-off gas must be actively managed, and sloshing loads in partially filled tanks are a key design consideration.

Unburned methane that escapes through the exhaust of gas-fuelled engines, most notably low-pressure four-stroke dual-fuel designs, with smaller contributions from crankcase venting and fuel handling. Because methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂, slip can erode much of the climate advantage LNG offers at the funnel. Engine makers have reduced slip substantially through combustion optimisation, and regulations such as FuelEU Maritime and the emerging IMO framework account for it by assessing emissions on a well-to-wake, CO₂-equivalent basis.

Methanol (CH₃OH) burned in dual-fuel engines, valued because it is liquid at ambient temperature and pressure and therefore needs only modest tank and piping modifications rather than cryogenic systems. It burns cleanly with very low sulphur and particulate emissions, and green e-methanol or biomethanol can cut well-to-wake greenhouse gas emissions substantially, which has driven a rapidly growing orderbook led by container shipping. As a toxic, low-flashpoint fuel it falls under the IGF Code framework via IMO interim guidelines, and its lower energy density requires roughly twice the tank volume of fuel oil for the same range.

Tier III is the strictest nitrogen oxide emission level under MARPOL Annex VI, applying to engines on ships constructed after the relevant dates when operating inside NOx Emission Control Areas such as the North Sea and Baltic. Most ships meet it using Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR), which injects a urea solution into the exhaust to convert NOx into nitrogen and water over a catalyst; exhaust gas recirculation is the main alternative. NOx compliance is separate from CO₂ regulation, and some alternative-fuel engines still need SCR to meet Tier III.

Systems that capture CO₂ from a ship's exhaust, typically using amine-based solvent scrubbing, then liquefy and store it on board for discharge ashore. OCCS could allow ships burning conventional or transitional fuels to cut emissions without switching fuel, but it demands significant energy, space and weight, and it depends on port infrastructure to receive and permanently store the captured CO₂. Pilot installations are in service and regulatory frameworks for crediting captured CO₂ are still being developed.

A small quantity of easily ignitable liquid fuel, usually marine gas oil, injected into a dual-fuel engine cylinder to ignite the main charge of gas or low-flashpoint fuel, which will not reliably self-ignite under compression. Pilot fuel typically accounts for a few percent or less of total energy input in gas mode, though the share varies by engine design and load. Because pilot fuel is fossil diesel, it is included when calculating a dual-fuel ship's overall emissions and fuel intensity.

A framework through which ship finance banks measure and publicly disclose how well the vessels in their loan portfolios align with IMO decarbonisation trajectories. Signatory lenders collect fuel consumption data from borrowers, calculate portfolio climate alignment scores and report them annually. The principles channel pressure for decarbonisation through access to capital, and parallel frameworks exist for marine insurers and for charterers (the Sea Cargo Charter).

The Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan, a mandatory ship-specific document under MARPOL Annex VI setting out how a vessel manages and improves its energy efficiency. Part I covers efficiency measures such as voyage optimisation and hull maintenance, Part II establishes the fuel data collection method for the IMO DCS, and Part III contains the ship's plan for achieving and maintaining its required Carbon Intensity Indicator rating. Ships rated D for three consecutive years or E in a single year must include corrective actions in a revised SEEMP.

Supplying a berthed ship with electricity from the shore grid so it can shut down its auxiliary engines, eliminating local emissions and noise in port. Also called cold ironing or onshore power supply (OPS), it requires standardised high-voltage connections on both ship and quay, and its climate benefit depends on the carbon intensity of the local grid. Regulation is accelerating uptake: EU rules will require container and passenger ships to use shore power in major EU ports from 2030, and Norwegian ports have invested heavily in OPS infrastructure.

The global limit on sulphur in marine fuel oil of 0.50% by mass, in force under MARPOL Annex VI since 1 January 2020, with a stricter 0.10% limit inside Emission Control Areas. Ships comply by burning very low sulphur fuel oil or distillates, or by fitting exhaust gas cleaning systems that allow continued use of high-sulphur fuel. The cap reshaped the bunker market almost overnight and remains the most sweeping fuel-quality regulation shipping has implemented; it targets air quality and health rather than greenhouse gases.

The portion of a fuel's lifecycle emissions released on board the ship, from the fuel tank through combustion or conversion to the propeller wash. It excludes upstream emissions from producing and transporting the fuel, which belong to the well-to-tank stage. A fuel can look attractive tank-to-wake yet perform poorly overall — hydrogen or ammonia made from fossil energy emits nothing at the funnel but carries a heavy upstream footprint — which is why regulators increasingly assess fuels well-to-wake.

An independent pressure-vessel tank, usually cylindrical or bilobe, used to store liquefied gas fuels such as LNG under the IGC and IGF Code tank classifications. Type C tanks can hold pressure build-up from boil-off gas for extended periods, simplifying gas management, and they need no secondary barrier, which makes them the most common choice for LNG-fuelled ships and smaller gas carriers. Their drawback is relatively poor use of hull volume compared with membrane or prismatic designs, limiting them to modest fuel capacities.

A blended residual fuel with a maximum sulphur content of 0.50%, developed so ships could meet the IMO 2020 sulphur cap without scrubbers or a switch to distillates. VLSFO rapidly became the dominant deep-sea bunker fuel, but its blended nature means quality and stability can vary between suppliers, so compatibility testing between bunkerings is prudent. It complies with sulphur rules while remaining a fossil fuel, so it is a baseline rather than a decarbonisation measure.

A lifecycle accounting boundary covering all greenhouse gas emissions of a marine fuel, from primary energy extraction and fuel production (well-to-tank) through onboard use (tank-to-wake). Well-to-wake assessment prevents emissions from simply being shifted upstream and is the basis on which FuelEU Maritime measures fuel GHG intensity, with the IMO's lifecycle assessment guidelines taking the same approach. Under this lens, the production pathway of a fuel — green versus grey hydrogen, biogenic versus fossil carbon — matters as much as what happens in the engine.

Technologies that harvest wind energy to supplement a ship's engines, including Flettner rotor sails, rigid wing sails, suction wings and kites. Depending on route, weather routing and installation size, they typically deliver fuel savings in the range of 5–20%, directly reducing emissions regardless of which fuel the ship burns. Wind assistance is recognised in efficiency frameworks such as EEDI/EEXI and FuelEU Maritime, and installations on tankers, bulkers and ro-ro vessels have grown steadily.

A ship that emits no greenhouse gases in operation, typically powered by batteries, hydrogen or other fuels used in ways that release no CO₂ on board. The term is often used loosely, so it matters whether a claim covers only tank-to-wake operation or the full well-to-wake lifecycle including fuel production. True zero- and near-zero-emission vessels are central to the IMO's 2050 ambition, and early examples — battery ferries, hydrogen ferries and small coastal tonnage — are concentrated in short-sea markets such as Norway.

terms.def: A power converter that uses actively controlled semiconductor switches (typically IGBTs) instead of a passive diode rectifier at the grid-facing side of a drive or battery converter. On ships, AFE converters allow power to flow in both directions, keep harmonic distortion low without bulky filters, and enable a battery to both charge from and discharge into the switchboard. They are a key building block of hybrid AC systems and onboard DC grids on OSVs and ferries.

The physical build-up of a marine battery system: individual electrochemical cells are grouped into modules, modules are stacked into racks (strings), and racks are combined into the complete shipboard ESS. Each level adds its own monitoring, fusing and disconnection functions, so a fault in one module or rack can be isolated without losing the whole system. Class rules and system design typically require that the vessel can tolerate the loss of one string while still meeting its safety functions.

An optional class notation confirming that a vessel's battery installation meets a classification society's rules for safety and, where applicable, for using the battery as a source of propulsion power. DNV, for example, distinguishes between Battery(Safety), covering installations where the battery is a supplementary source, and Battery(Power), where the battery is relied on as main or redundant power. The notations bring requirements for dedicated battery spaces, fire suppression, off-gas detection, ventilation and system testing.

The gradual, irreversible loss of a battery's capacity and increase in its internal resistance over time and use. Degradation is driven by cycling depth, charge/discharge rates, temperature and time at high state of charge, all of which the BMS and EMS try to manage. For a ferry or hybrid OSV it determines how many years the installed battery can still deliver its contracted crossing or spinning-reserve duty, and it is the basis for end-of-life and replacement planning.

The dedicated control and protection system supervising a battery installation cell by cell — monitoring voltage, current and temperature, balancing cells, and disconnecting the battery when limits are exceeded. The BMS is the primary safeguard against thermal runaway and the source of the state-of-charge and state-of-health data the vessel's EMS relies on.

The set of design measures protecting the dedicated compartment where a marine lithium-ion battery is installed. Class rules require batteries above small sizes to be placed in their own space with structural fire protection, a fixed fire-extinguishing system, off-gas detection and dedicated ventilation arranged to vent gases away from accommodation and machinery air intakes. The goal is to contain a thermal event to the battery space and protect the crew and the rest of the power plant.

A power plant that combines combustion engines with a battery energy storage system, letting the vessel run engines at optimal load, absorb load transients from the battery, and operate short periods on battery alone. On OSVs and ferries, hybridisation cuts fuel consumption, running hours and emissions — and in DP operation the ESS can act as instantly available spinning reserve.

The use of an ESS to instantly pick up load when a generator trips, preventing the frequency and voltage collapse that would otherwise black out the switchboard. Because a battery responds in milliseconds, far faster than a standby diesel can start and synchronise, it can carry the vessel through the disturbance or, after a blackout, re-energise the switchboard and support restart of the generators. On DP vessels this capability directly supports station-keeping integrity and is a core argument for battery hybridisation.

A measure of how fast a battery is charged or discharged relative to its capacity: 1C empties (or fills) the battery in one hour, 2C in half an hour. Marine ESS applications differ widely — spinning reserve demands short bursts at high C-rates, while zero-emission sailing draws lower rates for longer — and the chosen duty profile drives battery sizing, cooling and lifetime.

The specific component of battery degradation describing the reduction of usable energy capacity, usually expressed as a percentage of the original rated capacity. A marine battery is commonly considered to have reached end of life for its original duty when capacity has faded to around 70–80 percent of new. Vessel operators track capacity fade through the BMS and periodic capacity tests so that route energy budgets, DP reserve calculations and class documentation remain valid.

The process of evening out small state-of-charge differences between the series-connected cells in a battery string. Without balancing, the weakest cell limits the whole string, reaching its voltage limits first and forcing the system to stop charging or discharging early. The BMS performs balancing either passively, by bleeding energy from the highest cells through resistors, or actively, by shuttling energy between cells, preserving usable capacity and cell health over the system's life.

A thermal management arrangement in which battery modules are cooled by a sealed circuit of water-glycol coolant, with heat rejected to the ship's central fresh-water or seawater cooling system. Liquid cooling keeps cell temperatures within a narrow band even at high charge and discharge rates, which is essential for cycle life and for the fast charging used by battery ferries. It also decouples the battery space climate from the cells themselves, complementing the room's HVAC and ventilation functions.

The number of complete charge-discharge cycles a battery can deliver before its capacity fades to a defined end-of-life threshold, typically 70–80 percent of rated capacity. Cycle life depends strongly on depth of discharge, temperature and C-rate, so the same cells last far longer in a gentle spinning-reserve role than in heavy daily ferry cycling. Battery suppliers state cycle life under defined test conditions, and the EMS operating strategy is tuned to meet the vessel's required service years.

A power distribution architecture in which generators, batteries and consumers connect to a common DC bus instead of a fixed-frequency AC switchboard. DC grids let engines run at variable speed for better fuel efficiency, integrate batteries and fuel cells naturally, and reduce switchboard size — which is why they dominate modern hybrid OSV, ferry and fishing vessel designs.

The share of a battery's capacity that has been withdrawn in a discharge, expressed as a percentage; a battery discharged from 90 to 30 percent state of charge has seen a 60 percent DoD. Shallower cycling markedly extends cycle life, so marine systems are often operated within a restricted SoC window rather than from full to empty. DoD limits are set in the EMS strategy and reflected in the sizing margin of the installed battery.

The amount of energy a battery stores per unit of mass (Wh/kg) or volume (Wh/l). At system level, marine batteries deliver considerably less than the bare cell figure because modules, racks, cooling, fire protection and converters add weight and volume. Energy density drives how much zero-emission range a ferry can carry within its deadweight and stability limits, and it is one of the main trade-offs between cell chemistries.

The supervisory control layer that decides how a hybrid vessel's energy sources are used moment to moment — when to run engines, when to charge or discharge the battery, and how to split load for lowest fuel consumption or emissions. The EMS sits above the power management system and battery management system, optimising the plant against the vessel's operating mode.

The complete battery installation on board — cells, modules, racks, cooling, fire protection and the battery management system — engineered and class-approved as a single system. Marine ESS applications include spinning reserve, peak shaving, zero-emission harbour transits and blackout prevention, with class rules (e.g. DNV Battery notation) governing safety design and the crew training required to operate them.

The distinction between batteries optimised to store many kilowatt-hours (energy design) and batteries optimised to deliver high power relative to their capacity (power design). A battery ferry crossing a fjord needs an energy-optimised system for range, while a DP vessel using the battery for spinning reserve and peak shaving needs high C-rate power capability from a comparatively small pack. Cell selection, cooling and converter rating all follow from which duty dominates.

The improvement in a DP vessel's power system response achieved by adding fast energy storage to the plant. The battery absorbs and supplies the rapid thruster load fluctuations caused by waves and DP control action, so the diesel engines see a smoother load and the system rides through sudden steps without frequency dips. This allows fewer generators online for the same safety level and is recognised in hybrid class notations and DP capability documentation.

A power plant that pairs fuel cells, typically hydrogen-fuelled, with a battery so each source works where it is strongest. The fuel cell supplies steady base load at its efficient operating point, while the battery handles transients, peak loads and start-up, protecting the fuel cell stack from load steps that shorten its life. This architecture is central to emerging zero-emission ferries and short-sea vessels, with the EMS deciding the power split between the two sources.

The set of rules or optimisation logic the EMS uses to decide, at every moment, how load is shared between engines, batteries and other sources. Typical strategies include charge-sustaining operation around a target state of charge, load-dependent start and stop of generators, peak shaving thresholds and dedicated modes for DP, transit, harbour and zero-emission operation. A well-tuned strategy is what converts installed hybrid hardware into actual fuel, maintenance and emissions savings.

Operation of an electrical system with no connection to an external grid, which is the normal condition of a ship at sea. A vessel's power plant is effectively a small islanded microgrid: it must maintain its own voltage and frequency, balance generation against load in real time, and survive faults without outside support. Batteries strengthen an islanded system by providing instant reserve and, in DC-grid vessels, by helping form and stabilise the grid itself.

The two lithium-ion chemistries most common in marine service. NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) cells offer higher energy density, giving more kilowatt-hours per tonne, and have dominated marine installations to date. LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cells are heavier per kilowatt-hour but are generally more thermally stable, tolerate cycling well and avoid cobalt, and are increasingly considered for newbuilds. The choice affects weight, battery space size, fire safety case and lifetime cost.

A rechargeable battery based on lithium-ion cells, engineered and type-approved for shipboard installation. Compared with land or automotive systems, marine batteries add class-required layers of protection: marinised modules and racks, a certified BMS, dedicated battery spaces with fire suppression, off-gas detection and ventilation. Lithium-ion is the dominant technology behind hybrid OSVs, battery-electric ferries and DP spinning-reserve installations because of its high efficiency, energy density and fast response.

An EMS function in which the battery continuously smooths the load seen by the running engines, absorbing energy when demand dips and supplying it when demand rises. Where peak shaving targets occasional peaks, load levelling addresses the constant fluctuation of loads such as thrusters, cranes and heave-compensated winches. The engines can then run near a steady, efficient set point, reducing fuel consumption, exhaust emissions and mechanical wear.

Shore charging infrastructure capable of transferring power in the megawatt range, needed when a battery ferry must recover a full crossing's energy during a berth stay of only a few minutes. Norwegian fjord ferries pioneered this scale of charging, using automated connection systems, robotic plugs or induction, often supported by a shore-side battery buffer where the local grid is weak. High charge rates must be coordinated with the battery's C-rate limits and thermal management.

Monitoring of the battery space for the gases a lithium-ion cell vents in the early stage of failure, before or during thermal runaway. Detecting these gases gives the crew warning ahead of smoke or fire, allowing the affected string to be disconnected and ventilation and suppression measures to be activated. Class rules for battery notations require off-gas detection in battery spaces, with alarms integrated into the vessel's safety and automation systems.

Charging the battery in the short windows a vessel's schedule naturally provides, such as ferry berth stops, lock transits or cargo operations alongside, rather than in one long overnight session. It lets a modest battery support an energy-intensive timetable, but demands high charging power, reliable automated connection and careful thermal management. The EMS plans each charge so the vessel always departs with enough energy for the next leg plus reserves.

An energy management function where the battery supplies the top slice of short-duration load peaks, so the generators only need to cover the average demand. Typical shipboard peaks come from thruster bursts in DP, crane lifts or winch operations. Peak shaving allows fewer or smaller engines to run at an efficient, steady load, cutting fuel consumption, emissions and running hours; the battery recharges in the load troughs between peaks.

Battery systems or cells redeployed to a less demanding duty after they no longer meet the requirements of their first application, typically once capacity has faded to around 70–80 percent. A marine propulsion battery may find second life in shore-side energy storage or harbour charging buffers, spreading its embodied carbon and cost over more service years. Reuse on board is constrained by class type-approval and safety documentation, so most maritime second-life value today is realised ashore.

An electrical machine coupled to the main propulsion shaft or gearbox that can operate in two directions. In power take-off (PTO) mode it generates electricity from the efficient main engine, allowing auxiliary gensets to be shut down at sea; in power take-in (PTI) mode it works as a motor, boosting or taking over propulsion with power from gensets or the battery. Combined with frequency converters and an ESS, PTO/PTI is a cornerstone of modern hybrid machinery arrangements.

Transferring electrical energy from the shore grid into a vessel's battery while it is alongside, as distinct from shore power that merely feeds the hotel load. Charging systems range from manual cable connections for overnight charging to automated high-power systems that replenish a ferry in minutes at each berth. Norway's battery-electric ferry network is built on shore charging, and charger power, grid capacity and connection time are sizing parameters as important as the battery itself.

Standby power capacity available fast enough to cover the sudden loss of a running generator. Traditionally this meant keeping extra engines online at low load, particularly in DP operations, which burns fuel inefficiently and adds running hours. A battery certified for the duty can provide this reserve instead, responding in milliseconds, so the vessel can safely operate with fewer generators connected; class societies accept batteries as spinning reserve under the relevant battery and DP notations.

The energy currently stored in a battery expressed as a percentage of its present usable capacity, analogous to a fuel gauge. The BMS estimates SoC from cell voltages, current integration and temperature, and the EMS uses it to schedule charging, enforce operating windows and verify that reserves for DP or the next ferry crossing are in place. Because operating between roughly 20 and 90 percent extends cell life, marine systems rarely use the full 0–100 percent range in normal service.

A measure of a battery's condition relative to new, usually expressed as remaining capacity as a percentage of the original rated capacity, sometimes supplemented by internal resistance. SoH is tracked by the BMS and verified through periodic capacity testing, and it underpins class surveys, warranty claims and replacement planning. When SoH falls below the level needed for the vessel's duty, such as a full crossing or the certified spinning reserve, the system must be derated, augmented or replaced.

An energy storage device that stores charge electrostatically rather than chemically, giving very high power density, near-instant response and cycle life in the hundreds of thousands, but only a small amount of energy. In marine systems supercapacitors suit duties with rapid, repetitive power swings, such as crane and winch load smoothing or ride-through of momentary disturbances. They are sometimes combined with batteries so the supercapacitor absorbs the sharpest transients while the battery covers the energy.

A self-accelerating failure of a lithium-ion cell in which internal heating triggers chemical reactions that release more heat and flammable gases, potentially leading to fire and propagation to neighbouring cells. Triggers include internal defects, overcharge, external heating and mechanical damage. Marine battery design defends against it in layers: cell quality and BMS limits to prevent initiation, module design to resist propagation, and the battery space's off-gas detection, ventilation and fixed fire suppression to contain the consequences.

The portion of a battery's installed energy that is actually available for operations after subtracting the reserved margins at the top and bottom of the state-of-charge window, converter losses and any capacity held back for safety functions such as spinning reserve. A ferry with 2 MWh installed may plan its crossings on well under that figure. Distinguishing installed from usable energy is essential in tender specifications, route energy budgets and end-of-life assessments.

Running a generator set at whatever engine speed best matches the current load, instead of the fixed speed required to hold 50 or 60 Hz on a conventional AC switchboard. This is enabled by connecting the generator through power converters, most naturally on a DC-grid vessel, and it cuts fuel consumption markedly at the part loads where OSVs and ferries spend much of their time. Combined with an ESS, it lets each engine operate near its optimum while the battery handles transients.

An operating mode in which all propulsion and hotel load is supplied from the battery with every combustion engine stopped, producing no exhaust emissions and little noise. It is used for fjord crossings, harbour transits, port stays and environmentally restricted areas such as the Norwegian World Heritage fjords, where zero-emission requirements are being phased in. The EMS supervises the mode, ensuring enough energy remains to complete the planned operation and to restart engines or reach a charging point with margin.

categories.desc: The deepest maritime cybersecurity glossary online: IMO MSC.428(98), IACS UR E26/E27, USCG cyber rule, SBOM, OT security, threats, defences, governance — 300+ terms.

terms.def: A widely used guideline for resilient backups: keep three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy stored off-site. For a vessel this might mean the live system, a local backup server, and a copy replicated ashore when bandwidth allows. Following the rule ensures that a single event — ransomware, hardware failure, fire or flooding — cannot destroy every copy at once.

Cellular data links that ships use when operating near shore, often switching over automatically from satellite to save cost and gain bandwidth. Each cellular modem is an additional internet gateway that may bypass the ship's main firewall if not routed through the same security stack as the VSAT link. Vessels should treat 4G/LTE routers as untrusted perimeter devices: inventory them, disable default credentials, and ensure traffic passes through the ship's central firewall regardless of which bearer is active.

A framework combining three access-control functions: verifying who a user is (authentication), determining what they may do (authorisation), and recording what they actually did (accounting). Together these answer the questions "who logged in, what did they touch, and when" — essential for investigating incidents on ship and shore networks. On vessels, AAA is often weakened by shared bridge or engine-room accounts, which makes the accounting element meaningless.

A document that tells crew and shore staff what they may and may not do with company IT equipment, networks and internet connections. On board, it typically covers use of the vessel's business network, personal devices on crew Wi-Fi, USB sticks, social media and streaming over satellite links. A good acceptable use policy is short, written in plain language, and signed as part of onboarding so every seafarer knows the rules before they connect anything.

The practice of restricting who and what can use shipboard systems, networks and data, typically through user accounts, passwords, key cards and role-based permissions. On board, this means separating the master's administrative rights from crew accounts, limiting who can log on to bridge and engine-room workstations, and controlling vendor access to control systems. Weak access control, such as shared passwords on ECDIS or automation stations, remains one of the most common findings in maritime cyber audits.

A rule that temporarily disables a user account after a set number of failed login attempts, blocking password-guessing and brute-force attacks. Lockout policies need careful tuning in maritime settings: locking the shared ECDIS or DP operator account at a critical moment could create a safety problem worse than the one being prevented. Many fleets therefore combine short lockout timers with alerting rather than indefinite lockouts on operational systems.

A well-resourced attacker, often state-backed, that gains long-term covert access to a network and pursues a specific objective over months or years. In the maritime sector, APTs typically target shipping companies, ports and shipbuilders for cargo data, vessel movements, sanctioned-trade intelligence or naval technology. Their hallmark is patience: quiet reconnaissance and persistence rather than immediate, visible damage.

Techniques for deceiving or degrading machine-learning systems, for example by feeding them subtly manipulated inputs that cause misclassification. For autonomous and remotely operated vessels this is a direct safety concern: a perception system trained to recognise buoys, small craft or navigation marks could be fooled by crafted visual patterns or poisoned training data. Testing perception and decision systems against adversarial inputs is becoming part of assurance work for autonomous shipping.

The use of machine learning to support security operations, typically by detecting unusual behaviour in network traffic, user activity or system logs faster than human analysts could. In a fleet context, AI-assisted monitoring can flag anomalies across many vessels with limited bandwidth and no onboard security staff. It is a support tool rather than a replacement for skilled analysts: models generate false positives and still require people who understand both the technology and shipboard operations to judge what matters.

Cyber attacks that use artificial intelligence to increase their scale, speed or credibility — for example convincingly written phishing emails in any language, voice cloning of a company executive to authorise a payment, or automated discovery of vulnerable systems. For shipping companies the practical effect is that crude, easily spotted fraud attempts are being replaced by polished ones referencing real vessels, ports and counterparties. Defences shift towards verification procedures that do not depend on how genuine a message looks or sounds.

A security measure in which a critical system, such as a vessel's automation or cargo control network, has no physical or wireless connection to other networks or the internet. An air gap greatly reduces remote attack risk, but it is rarely absolute on modern ships: USB sticks used for chart updates, vendor laptops and retrofitted remote-monitoring links routinely bridge supposedly isolated systems. Crews should treat an air gap as one layer of protection to be verified regularly, not as a guarantee of safety.

The transmission of false Automatic Identification System messages to create ghost vessels, hide a ship's true identity or falsify its reported position. Because AIS was designed without authentication, spoofed targets can appear on ECDIS and radar overlays and mislead watchkeepers, VTS operators and fleet tracking services. Bridge teams should cross-check AIS data against radar, visual observation and other independent sources before acting on it.

The discipline of ensuring that alarms from engine room, bridge, and automation systems remain trustworthy and manageable, including under cyber attack. An attacker who can suppress, delay, or flood alarms can hide a developing machinery failure or overwhelm the watchkeeper with nuisance alarms until real ones are ignored. Security-aware alarm management means protecting alarm servers and networks from tampering, logging alarm inhibits and acknowledgements, and training crew to treat unexplained alarm floods or silences as possible cyber events, not just software glitches.

The gradual desensitisation that sets in when people receive too many warnings, most of which turn out to be false alarms. Watchkeepers already know this from bridge and engine room alarm systems, and the same effect applies to security alerts: if an antivirus or monitoring tool cries wolf constantly, the one alert that matters gets dismissed too. Reducing alert fatigue means tuning systems so alarms are few, meaningful and actionable.

Software that detects, blocks and removes malicious programs such as viruses, worms, trojans and ransomware, using known signatures and behavioural analysis. On ships, antivirus is a first line of defence on crew computers, planning stations and any system exposed to USB sticks or email. Its main limitation at sea is that signature updates depend on connectivity, so vessels with infrequent updates should not rely on antivirus alone.

Protecting the application programming interfaces (APIs) through which shipboard systems, fleet platforms, ports and third-party services exchange data — voyage plans, performance data, noon reports, cargo information. Weakly secured APIs can expose fleet data at scale or provide a path from a shore platform toward vessel systems. Good practice includes strong authentication for every API call, limiting each integration to the data it actually needs, and logging access so misuse can be detected.

A control that allows only pre-approved software to run on a computer, blocking everything else by default. It is well suited to shipboard OT and navigation workstations, which run a fixed set of applications and change rarely, unlike office PCs. On an ECDIS or automation station, whitelisting can stop malware introduced via USB from executing even when antivirus signatures are out of date.

The practice of maintaining an accurate, up-to-date inventory of all hardware, software and network connections across the fleet — from office servers to the ECDIS, engine control systems and every switch in between. You cannot protect what you do not know you have, so the asset register is the foundation for patching, risk assessment and incident response. For ships this includes recording which systems are onboard each vessel, their software versions, and who is responsible for maintaining them.

The practice of charting the realistic routes an attacker could take from an initial foothold — a phishing email, a compromised supplier, an exposed remote-access service — to a valuable target such as a vessel's automation network or a company's finance system. For ships, typical paths run through business networks, remote-maintenance connections and shared USB media into OT systems. Mapping these paths shows which defences actually break the chain, helping prioritise limited security budgets.

The sum of all points where an attacker could try to enter or extract data from a vessel's systems, including satellite links, crew Wi-Fi, USB ports, vendor remote-access connections and shore-side fleet management platforms. Every new connected device, from smart sensors to remote engine monitoring, enlarges the attack surface of the ship. Mapping and reducing this surface, for example by disabling unused ports and services, is a first step in any shipboard cyber risk assessment.

The process of verifying that a user, device or system is who or what it claims to be, typically with passwords, cryptographic keys, certificates or biometrics. It is the gatekeeper for everything else in security: authorisation decisions are only meaningful if the identity behind them is genuine. Shipboard practice has historically been weak here — shared logins on bridge and ECDIS workstations are common — and tightening authentication is one of the most cost-effective improvements a shipping company can make.

The process of deciding what an authenticated user or system is allowed to do — which files to read, which settings to change, which systems to reach. It follows the principle of least privilege: people and software should have only the access their role requires. On a vessel this means, for example, that a crew welfare laptop should never be able to reach the automation network, and a service technician's remote account should open only the specific system under maintenance.

The security discipline for vessels operated with reduced crew, remote control or full autonomy, where a cyber compromise can translate directly into loss of navigational control. Because there may be no crew aboard to intervene, the integrity of sensors, decision software and the ship-shore communication link becomes safety-critical, and requirements for redundancy, secure fallback states and link protection are correspondingly stricter. Classification societies and flag states increasingly treat cybersecurity as a core element of approving autonomous operations, alongside traditional seaworthiness.

A hidden way into a system that bypasses normal authentication, either planted by an attacker or left behind as an undocumented vendor access path. On vessels, forgotten remote-maintenance accounts in ECDIS, automation or DP systems can act as de facto backdoors. Once in place, a backdoor lets an attacker return at will, even after the original vulnerability is patched.

The process of keeping secure copies of critical data and system configurations so they can be restored after a cyber incident, hardware failure or ransomware attack. For ships this covers ECDIS charts and routes, loading computer data, PMS records and automation system configurations, with at least one copy kept offline or ashore. Recovery procedures should be tested periodically, since a backup that has never been restored under drill conditions may fail when it is needed at sea.

Protection of the PLC-controlled treatment plants (UV, electrochlorination, or filtration) that ships must run to meet the Ballast Water Management Convention. These systems are often installed as retrofit packages with their own controllers, remote-support modems, and USB service ports, and are easily overlooked in the ship's cyber inventory. Compromise or malfunction can interfere with ballast operations, affect stability planning, and create port state control problems if treatment records are corrupted.

A single, hardened computer that acts as the controlled entry point into a protected network — all remote sessions must pass through it before reaching anything inside. In fleet operations, a jump server is the standard way to let vendors or shore engineers reach onboard automation or DP systems: they log in to the bastion, are authenticated and recorded, and only then connect onward. Because it concentrates all access in one place, it is heavily monitored and stripped of unnecessary software.

Protecting the large volumes of operational data modern fleets generate — fuel consumption, engine telemetry, positions, weather routing, cargo records — as it is collected on board, transmitted ashore and analysed in cloud platforms. This data has commercial value: aggregated voyage and performance data can reveal charter strategies, cargo flows and technical condition to competitors or attackers. Security concerns include who owns the data, which third parties (engine makers, analytics vendors, charterers) can access it, and whether its integrity can be trusted for decisions such as performance claims or emissions reporting.

terms.term: BIMCO Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships
terms.def: An industry guidance document produced by BIMCO together with other shipping associations, offering practical advice on identifying, protecting against and responding to cyber threats on board. The guidelines translate high-level frameworks into shipboard terms, covering topics such as network layout, remote access, crew awareness and incident response. Many companies use them as the working reference when implementing IMO cyber risk requirements in their safety management systems.

Verifying identity using a physical characteristic — fingerprint, face or iris — instead of, or in addition to, a password. Biometrics are convenient because they cannot be forgotten or easily shared, which suits shipboard environments where crew rotate frequently and shared passwords are a chronic weakness. They work best as one factor in multi-factor authentication rather than as the sole means of access.

The use of distributed-ledger technology in shipping — most visibly for electronic bills of lading and cargo documentation — viewed through a security lens. A blockchain makes recorded entries very hard to alter afterwards, which suits documents of title, but it does not guarantee that data was correct when entered, and the surrounding platforms, user accounts and private keys remain conventional attack targets. In practice the security of a blockchain-based shipping service depends far more on the operator's platform security and key management than on the ledger itself.

The defenders: the people responsible for monitoring systems, detecting intrusions and responding to attacks, whether real or simulated. In a shipping company the blue team role may sit with the IT department, a managed security provider, or a fleet operations centre watching vessel networks. During security exercises the blue team practises spotting and containing the red team's simulated attacks.

A network of compromised computers or devices controlled remotely by an attacker, often used to send spam, mine cryptocurrency or launch denial-of-service attacks. Shipboard PCs and poorly secured connected devices can be silently recruited into botnets, consuming scarce satellite bandwidth and exposing the vessel's network to further compromise. Unusual outbound traffic over the VSAT link is a common first sign that an onboard machine has been enrolled in a botnet.

An attack that tries many password or key combinations, often automatically, until one works. Internet-exposed services common in shipping, such as remote-access portals, VSAT management interfaces and crew webmail, are routine brute-force targets. Strong passwords, account lockouts and multi-factor authentication make this approach largely impractical.

Structured ways for outside researchers to report security flaws they find in a company's systems or products. A responsible disclosure policy gives researchers a safe, legal channel to report a vulnerability so it can be fixed before it is exploited; a bug bounty adds a financial reward. For maritime suppliers of navigation, automation or fleet software, having a disclosure route matters — without one, a researcher who finds a flaw in a widely installed shipboard system has no good way to warn anyone.

A documented plan for keeping essential operations running when a major disruption hits — including a cyber attack that takes down email, planning systems or vessel communications. For a shipping company this means knowing how to charter, crew, bunker and communicate with vessels using fallback methods such as phone, paper and alternative channels. The plan should be tested regularly, because a BCP that only exists on the same server the attackers just encrypted is no plan at all.

Fraud in which attackers use a compromised or convincingly spoofed business email account to trick staff into making payments or changing bank details. Shipping is a prime target because large payments to unfamiliar counterparties are normal: bunker invoices, charter hire, port disbursements and agency fees. A typical maritime BEC asks the accounts team to pay a legitimate-looking invoice to a "updated" bank account controlled by the criminals. Verifying payment changes through a second, independent channel is the standard defence.

A structured exercise that works out which business processes and systems matter most, and what it would cost — in money, safety and reputation — if each one were unavailable for hours, days or weeks. The results drive sensible priorities: it tells you whether the crewing system, the planned maintenance system or the charter party archive needs faster recovery. For vessel operations it also identifies which onboard systems a ship can safely sail without, and for how long.
