categories.desc: Autonomous shipping terms explained: MASS, IMO MASS Code, autonomy degrees, remote operations centres, sensor fusion, collision avoidance, ODD and more.

terms.def: The distinction between a system that executes pre-programmed functions under human supervision (automation) and one that can sense its environment, evaluate options and select actions to meet a goal (autonomy). An autopilot holding a set heading is automation; a system that re-plans its own route around traffic is exercising autonomy. The distinction matters in ship design and regulation because responsibility, approval requirements and operator training differ depending on how much decision-making authority the machine holds.

The software stack that lets a vessel plan and execute its own voyage: sensor fusion builds a picture of surrounding traffic and hazards, a collision-avoidance engine evaluates COLREG-compliant manoeuvres, and a control layer commands propulsion and steering. ANS installations today typically operate under crew or remote supervision, with authority handed back to humans in defined conditions.

The IMO's four-step scale for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships: Degree One — crewed ship with automated processes and decision support; Degree Two — remotely controlled with seafarers on board; Degree Three — remotely controlled with no seafarers on board; Degree Four — fully autonomous, with the ship's systems making decisions themselves. The scale frames how rules, manning and liability apply as autonomy increases.

The body of evidence and processes used to demonstrate that autonomy software — including decision logic and machine-learning components — behaves safely and predictably across its intended operating conditions. Because software failures in an autonomous vessel cannot be caught by an onboard crew, assurance relies on structured development processes, extensive simulation, code and model verification, and independent review by classification societies or flag administrations. It is a central topic in the approval of MASS designs.

An onboard system that detects other vessels and obstacles, assesses collision risk, and either advises on or automatically executes avoiding manoeuvres. In autonomous ships it combines data from radar, AIS, cameras and other sensors with decision algorithms that must produce manoeuvres consistent with the COLREGs. Its reliability under poor visibility, dense traffic and sensor degradation is one of the most heavily tested aspects of any MASS design.

The requirement that autonomous and remotely operated vessels manoeuvre in accordance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, the same rules that govern crewed ships. This is technically demanding because the COLREGs were written for human judgement and include qualitative concepts such as "ordinary practice of seamen" and "ample time", which algorithms must interpret in ways other mariners find predictable. Demonstrating COLREG-compliant behaviour in mixed traffic is a core element of MASS trials and approvals.

The time delay between a signal being sent and received over a communication link, for example between a vessel and a remote operations centre. Latency affects how quickly a remote operator perceives events on board and how quickly commands take effect, which constrains what tasks can safely be performed remotely. Satellite links typically introduce more latency than coastal 4G/5G coverage, so latency budgets are a key input when defining a remotely operated vessel's operating area and fallback behaviour.

The use of cameras and image-processing algorithms to let a vessel's systems recognise and track objects such as ships, buoys, kayaks, floating debris and shorelines. Computer vision complements radar and AIS by detecting small or non-transmitting targets and by classifying what a contact actually is. Maritime conditions — glare, rain, fog, darkness and sea clutter — make robust performance difficult, which is why vision is normally fused with other sensor types rather than used alone.

The provision of multiple independent communication links — for example satellite, 4G/5G and dedicated radio — so that a remotely supervised vessel does not depend on a single connection to shore. If the primary link degrades or fails, traffic switches to a backup link, and if all links are lost the vessel must transition to a predefined safe fallback behaviour. Redundancy requirements are typically derived from a risk assessment of the vessel's operating area and autonomy level.

terms.term: Cyber Risk Management for Autonomous Ships
terms.def: The identification, assessment and mitigation of cyber threats to autonomous and remotely operated vessels, whose navigation, machinery and communication systems are software-defined and connected to shore. Because control commands travel over networks, threats include spoofed sensor data, hijacked communication links and compromised remote operations centres. Mitigations include encrypted and authenticated links, network segregation, monitoring, and designing the vessel to enter a safe state if its systems detect tampering or lose trusted communication.

A continuously updated digital model of a vessel or system, fed by live sensor data, that mirrors the physical asset's condition and behaviour. Digital twins support performance optimisation, predictive maintenance and remote diagnostics, and provide the simulation backbone for testing autonomous functions and training crews on vessel-specific scenarios.

A continuous, automated evaluation of operational risk during a voyage, updating as traffic, weather, system health and position change. In autonomous vessels, dynamic risk assessment allows the control system or remote operators to adapt speed, route or autonomy level to the current situation — for example slowing down when sensor confidence drops in fog. It contrasts with the static, pre-voyage risk assessments traditionally used in shipping.

An IMO-led concept for the harmonised collection, integration and exchange of maritime information by electronic means, on board and ashore, to improve berth-to-berth navigation and related services. E-navigation covers standardised data formats, digital route exchange, and improved communication between ships and shore services. It is an important enabler for autonomous shipping, since MASS depend on reliable, machine-readable navigational information and structured ship-to-shore data flows.

The use of virtual geographic boundaries to constrain where a vessel may operate or what behaviour is permitted within a defined area. An autonomous vessel's control system can be configured to remain inside an approved operating area, avoid exclusion zones, or change speed and autonomy mode when crossing a boundary. Geofencing is commonly used in test areas and port approaches to keep trials within permitted waters.

A control arrangement in which a human must review or approve an automated system's decisions before they are executed. In maritime autonomy this typically means the system proposes a manoeuvre and an operator, on board or ashore, confirms it. Related concepts are human-on-the-loop, where the human supervises and can intervene but the system acts on its own, and human-out-of-the-loop, where the system operates without real-time human involvement. The chosen arrangement shapes operator workload, latency requirements and regulatory approval.

The International Maritime Organization's goal-based instrument setting out safety requirements for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships, covering areas such as remote operation, autonomous functions, connectivity and the role of the human operator. The first, non-mandatory version of the Code was adopted at MSC 111 in 2026, with a voluntary experience-building phase beginning around July 2026. A mandatory MASS Code is intended to follow, expected around 2030–2032, informed by lessons from the voluntary phase.

A sensing technology that measures distances by emitting laser pulses and timing their reflections, producing a precise three-dimensional point cloud of the surroundings. On autonomous vessels, lidar is used for close-range perception tasks such as docking, detecting small objects near the hull and mapping quaysides, where radar resolution is insufficient. Its range is shorter than radar and its performance degrades in heavy rain or fog, so it is typically one element of a fused sensor suite.

The use of algorithms that learn patterns from data rather than following fully hand-written rules, applied in shipping to tasks such as object classification in camera images, trajectory prediction of nearby traffic, predictive maintenance and route optimisation. In autonomous vessels, machine learning most often appears inside the perception system. Because learned behaviour is difficult to specify exhaustively, its use in safety functions raises particular verification and assurance challenges that regulators and classification societies are actively addressing.

The IMO's term for a surface ship that can operate with some degree of independence from human interaction, ranging from ships with automated decision support and crew on board to fully autonomous vessels. The IMO describes this range using four degrees of autonomy, and a single voyage may involve several degrees at different stages. MASS is the umbrella concept under which international regulation, including the IMO MASS Code, is being developed.

A predefined state an autonomous vessel transitions to when it can no longer continue its planned operation safely — for example after losing critical sensors, propulsion redundancy or the link to its remote operations centre. Typical minimum risk conditions include stopping and holding position, anchoring, or proceeding slowly to a designated safe location. Defining credible fallback behaviours for every foreseeable failure, and proving the vessel can reach them, is a fundamental part of MASS safety design and approval.

terms.term: Norwegian Test Areas for Autonomous Ships
terms.def: Designated sea areas in Norway where autonomous vessel technology can be tested under agreed conditions with the support of the maritime authorities. The first, in Trondheimsfjorden, was established in 2016, and further fjord test beds followed, reflecting Norway's sheltered coastal waters, strong maritime cluster and cooperative regulators. These areas have hosted trials ranging from small research craft to commercial projects and have contributed operational experience feeding into international MASS regulation.

The specific set of conditions under which an autonomous function is designed to work safely — including geographic area, weather and sea state limits, traffic density, visibility, and required connectivity. A vessel's autonomy is only valid inside its ODD; if conditions drift outside it, the system must hand control to a human or enter a minimum risk condition. Precisely defining and monitoring the ODD is central to approving and operating autonomous vessels.

The process by which an autonomous vessel computes a safe, efficient trajectory from its current position toward its destination, taking into account charted depths, traffic, weather, vessel manoeuvring characteristics and the COLREGs. Path planning typically works on two levels: voyage-level route planning done in advance, and local re-planning that continuously adjusts the track to avoid other vessels and obstacles. The output feeds the vessel's track control and collision avoidance functions.

The collection of sensors and processing software that builds an autonomous vessel's model of its surroundings — detecting, classifying and tracking vessels, obstacles, navigation marks and the shoreline. A typical maritime perception system fuses radar, AIS, optical and infrared cameras, lidar and GNSS positioning. Its output, often called a world model, is what the vessel's decision-making functions act on, so perception reliability directly bounds how much autonomy can safely be granted.

An operating concept in which a crewed vessel's bridge is left without a watchkeeper for defined periods, with automated navigation and lookout systems maintaining the watch and alerting crew when human intervention is needed. It is seen as a practical intermediate step toward higher autonomy, allowing reduced bridge manning at night or in open water while crew remain on board. Approval depends on demonstrating that the automated watch performs at least as well as a human lookout within the permitted conditions.

An operating concept in which the machinery spaces run without continuous local supervision for defined periods, relying on automation, condition monitoring and alarm systems, with engineers on call. Long established in conventional shipping through unattended machinery space (UMS) class notations, it takes on new significance for autonomous vessels, where machinery may need to operate for entire voyages with no one on board. This pushes requirements for machinery redundancy, remote diagnostics and automated response to faults.

A shore-based facility from which operators monitor, supervise and when necessary control one or more vessels via communication links. A ROC typically presents sensor feeds, navigation displays, system health data and alarm handling, and may allow direct remote manoeuvring. Its design raises questions familiar from bridge design — workload, alertness, handover procedures and how many vessels one operator can safely oversee — and it is a central element of the operational concepts addressed by the IMO MASS Code.

The knowledge, skills and certification needed by personnel who supervise or control vessels from shore. Remote operators need traditional seamanship and COLREG understanding, plus new competences: interpreting sensor and system-health data, managing degraded communication links, supervising several vessels, and taking over control safely mid-situation. Formal international competence standards are still developing alongside the MASS regulatory framework, and simulator-based training is expected to play a major role, much as it does for bridge and DP operators today.

A condition in which a vessel poses minimal risk to people, the environment and other traffic, which an autonomous system must be able to reach and maintain after a failure. Depending on the vessel and location, a safe state may mean drifting clear of traffic with lights and signals active, holding position on thrusters, or being anchored. The concept underpins fallback design: every identified failure scenario should have a defined path to a safe state that does not rely on onboard crew.

The coordinated organisation of vessel traffic through shared voyage information, route exchange and shore-based services, extending the role of traditional vessel traffic services (VTS). By letting ships and shore centres exchange intended routes and timing digitally, sea traffic management improves predictability in congested waters. For autonomous vessels it offers a structured, machine-readable traffic picture, which is easier for autonomy systems to use than informal VHF coordination between human watchkeepers.

The combining of data from multiple sensor types — such as radar, AIS, optical and infrared cameras, lidar and GNSS — into a single consistent picture of the vessel's surroundings. Fusion exploits the complementary strengths of each sensor: radar works in fog, cameras classify targets, AIS identifies transmitting ships. It also provides cross-checking, so that a false or failed reading from one sensor can be detected against the others, which is essential for trusting an autonomous vessel's world model.

Continuous observation of a vessel's navigation, machinery and system status from a facility ashore, without necessarily exercising direct control. Monitoring is the lightest form of shore involvement in vessel operation: operators watch health data and alarms and can escalate to advisory contact or remote control if something develops. It is used both for autonomous vessels and, increasingly, for conventional ships as a fleet-support function, and it forms the baseline activity of a remote operations centre.

The perception of what is happening around a vessel, the understanding of what it means, and the projection of how the situation will develop — classically described as three levels applied to a navigator's watch. In autonomous shipping the term covers both the machine's situational awareness, built by its perception system, and the remote operator's awareness, which must be maintained through displays and data links rather than direct senses. Degraded operator awareness during remote supervision is a recognised human-factors risk.

A set of cameras mounted to give full or near-360-degree visual coverage around a vessel, feeding both machine perception and remote operator displays. Arrays typically combine daylight cameras with infrared or thermal cameras so that small craft, persons in the water and unlit objects can be detected in darkness and poor visibility. Stitched panoramic views from such arrays are a primary way remote operators regain the out-of-window view they lose by not being on board.

Direct human control of a vessel's steering, propulsion and other functions from a location off the ship, usually a remote operations centre, over a communication link. Teleoperation corresponds to the IMO's remotely controlled degrees of autonomy and is distinct from autonomous operation, where the vessel's own systems make decisions. Its safety depends heavily on link quality: latency, bandwidth and reliability determine how faithfully the operator perceives the situation and how promptly commands reach the vessel.

A surface craft designed to operate with no one on board, controlled remotely, operating autonomously, or combining both. USVs range from small survey and inspection craft to larger vessels for offshore support, ocean data collection and defence tasks. Because they carry no crew, their design can dispense with accommodation and life-saving arrangements, but they depend entirely on their perception systems, communication links and fallback logic — and, lacking an onboard lookout, they face the same COLREG-compliance questions as larger MASS.

The paired activities of confirming that an autonomous function is built correctly to its specification (verification) and that it actually behaves safely in its intended operating conditions (validation). Because real-world sea trials cannot cover every traffic and weather combination, validation relies heavily on simulation-based testing across large scenario libraries, complemented by controlled trials in designated test areas. Classification societies and flag states use the resulting evidence when approving autonomous vessels and their operating envelopes.

A Norwegian battery-electric container ship developed by fertiliser producer Yara with Kongsberg, and operated with the involvement of Massterly, carrying cargo on a short coastal route in southern Norway. Conceived to replace truck transport between Yara's plant and nearby ports, the vessel has operated with a progressively reduced crew as technology and procedures are proven, serving as a testbed for autonomous coastal shipping. It is one of the most cited real-world reference projects in the international MASS debate.

terms.def: The control and treatment of ballast water to prevent the transfer of invasive aquatic species between regions, governed by the IMO Ballast Water Management Convention. Ships must carry an approved management plan, keep records, and meet discharge standards, usually by installing a treatment system.

An independent body — such as DNV, Lloyd's Register, ABS or Bureau Veritas — that sets technical rules for ship design, construction and maintenance, and surveys vessels against them. Class notation determines a DP vessel's equipment class (DP 1/2/3), and classification is in practice a prerequisite for insurance and flag registration.

The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 — the global "rules of the road" defining conduct between vessels, right of way, lights, shapes and sound signals. Every watchkeeping officer must know them thoroughly, and they are examined in depth for every Certificate of Competency.

The country in which a vessel is registered and whose laws govern it. The flag state issues certificates, sets manning requirements, endorses Certificates of Competency and is responsible for enforcing IMO conventions on its ships — either directly or through recognised organisations such as classification societies.

The trade association for offshore marine contractors, publishing widely adopted guidance on DP operations, diving, surveys and marine assurance — including the influential M-series documents on DP FMEAs, annual trials and incident reporting. IMCA guidance is not law, but charterers and auditors treat much of it as the de facto industry standard.

The United Nations agency responsible for the safety, security and environmental performance of international shipping. The IMO produces the conventions that frame the industry — SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, COLREGs — which member flag states then implement and enforce in national law.

The International Safety Management Code, which requires every shipping company to run a documented Safety Management System covering safe operation, emergency preparedness, incident reporting and continuous improvement. Compliance is certified through company (DOC) and ship (SMC) audits, and the ISM Code is where "safety culture" becomes an auditable obligation.

The International Ship and Port Facility Security Code, adopted after 9/11, which mandates security assessments, ship security plans, designated security officers and graduated security levels (1–3) for ships and ports. It is implemented through SOLAS Chapter XI-2 and verified by flag and port state inspection.

The marks on a ship's side (the "Plimsoll mark") showing the maximum permitted draught in different zones and seasons, established by the International Load Line Convention. They guarantee minimum freeboard and reserve buoyancy for the conditions the vessel will meet.

The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, structured in six annexes covering oil, noxious liquids, packaged harmful substances, sewage, garbage and air emissions. MARPOL drives everything from oily-water separator rules to the sulphur cap and EEXI/CII carbon measures.

The IMO's "Guidelines for vessels and units with dynamic positioning (DP) systems" (2017), which updated the original MSC/Circ.645 framework. It defines the three DP equipment classes and functional requirements for new vessels, and is the reference point that class rules and industry guidance build upon.

Norway's flag and coastal state administration, responsible for ship registration (NOR/NIS registers), certification of Norwegian seafarers, and supervision of vessel safety and the working environment. For companies operating from Norway — including the offshore cluster around Ålesund — the NMA is the primary regulatory interface.

The inspection of foreign ships in national ports to verify compliance with international conventions, coordinated regionally through memoranda of understanding such as Paris MoU and Tokyo MoU. Deficiencies can lead to detention, and a company's PSC record directly affects its commercial standing.

The structured identification of hazards, evaluation of their likelihood and consequence, and definition of control measures before work is carried out. On ships this ranges from task-level toolbox assessments to formal HAZID/HAZOP studies for marine operations, and it is a cornerstone requirement of the ISM Code.

The company-wide framework of policies, procedures, responsibilities and audits required by the ISM Code to ensure safe ship operation and pollution prevention. The SMS is where regulations, manufacturer instructions and company experience are turned into the procedures crews actually follow.

The International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea — the most important maritime safety treaty, covering construction, fire protection, life-saving appliances, radio communications, navigation safety and management. Most other safety instruments, from the ISM Code to the ISPS Code, are implemented as SOLAS chapters.

categories.intro: Maritime training terms explained: STCW, Certificate of Competency, DPO certification, CPD, simulator training, e-learning, competence assessment and more.
categories.title: Maritime Training & Certification Glossary — STCW, CoC, DPO & E-Learning Terms | Maritime.Studio
categories.desc: Maritime training terms explained: STCW, Certificate of Competency, DPO certification, CPD, simulator training, e-learning, competence assessment and more.

terms.def: A human-factors discipline that trains bridge teams to use all available resources — people, procedures, equipment and information — effectively and to communicate without ambiguity. BRM training addresses workload management, challenge-and-response culture and error trapping, and is embedded in STCW requirements for deck officers.

The licence issued by a flag state administration confirming that a seafarer meets the STCW standards of knowledge, skill and sea service for a given rank — for example Officer of the Watch, Chief Mate or Master. CoCs must be revalidated periodically, which drives much of the recurring demand for maritime refresher training.

A structured evaluation of whether a seafarer can actually perform a task to a defined standard, using evidence such as simulator exercises, onboard observation, oral questioning and written tests. Modern competence management systems track assessments over time, closing the gap between holding a certificate and demonstrating skill.

The ongoing, documented learning a maritime professional undertakes throughout their career — refresher courses, e-learning modules, seminars and structured onboard experience. CPD is increasingly formalised in schemes such as the Nautical Institute's DP logbook requirements, and is central to keeping competence current between certificate revalidations.

Structured online training delivered through web platforms and learning management systems, allowing seafarers to study ashore or on board without travelling to a classroom. Well-designed maritime e-learning combines regulation-aligned content, interactive scenarios and assessment — the model behind Maritime.Studio's online programmes for officers and DPOs.

The mandatory onboard training a crew member receives when joining a vessel, covering safety arrangements, emergency duties and the specific equipment fitted — before being assigned shipboard duties. For DP vessels this extends to vessel-specific DP familiarisation covering the power plant, control system and ASOG.

The software platform that hosts, delivers and tracks training content — enrolments, progress, assessments and certificates — for a fleet or training provider. A good maritime LMS gives shore management live visibility of crew competence status and automates revalidation reminders.

Training delivered in short, focused units — typically 3 to 10 minutes each — designed around a single learning objective. Microlearning suits seafarers' fragmented time on board and measurably improves retention when used for refreshers, pre-task briefings and spaced repetition of critical procedures.

The most widely recognised certification pathway for DP operators, combining an induction course, logged DP seatime, a simulator course, further seatime and a final assessment, recorded in the NI DP logbook. It issues the DP Certificate most charterers and vetting schemes expect, with revalidation requirements that keep DPO experience current.

Training conducted in full-mission bridge, engine room or DP simulators that reproduce vessel behaviour, equipment interfaces and failure scenarios realistically. Simulators let crews practise emergencies — drive-offs, blackouts, reference failures — that could never be rehearsed safely at sea, and are integral to DPO certification and BRM courses.

The International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers, which sets the global minimum standards for seafarer competence, certification, medical fitness and rest hours. Every Certificate of Competency, ancillary course and refresher requirement traces back to the STCW Convention and Code, as amended in Manila 2010.

The systematic comparison of the competences a role requires against the competences the people in it currently hold, producing a prioritised training plan. A rigorous TNA keeps training budgets pointed at genuine risk and performance gaps rather than generic course catalogues.

Immersive training delivered through VR headsets that place the learner inside a realistic 3D environment — an engine room, a deck operation, a lifeboat launch — where procedures and hazards can be practised safely and repeatedly. VR complements full-mission simulators by making experiential training portable and dramatically cheaper per seat.

categories.desc: Vessel operations terms explained: passage planning, under-keel clearance, tonnage, offshore vessel types (PSV, AHTS, MODU), pilotage, VTS and more.

terms.term: AHTS — Anchor Handling Tug Supply vessel
terms.def: An offshore vessel designed to deploy, recover and relocate anchors and mooring systems for drilling rigs and floating installations, while also carrying deck cargo and supplies. AHTS vessels combine high bollard pull with dynamic positioning capability, making them among the most demanding platforms for DP operators.

A transponder system that automatically broadcasts a vessel's identity, position, course and speed to nearby ships and shore stations via VHF. SOLAS requires AIS on virtually all commercial vessels over 300 GT on international voyages, and it is a primary tool for collision avoidance and traffic monitoring.

An empirical scale from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane) that relates wind speed to observed sea conditions. It remains a common shorthand in weather forecasts, passage planning and operational limits for marine activities.

The maximum pulling force a vessel can exert at zero speed, measured in tonnes during a certified bollard pull test. It is the headline capability figure for tugs and anchor handlers, and directly determines what towing and mooring operations a vessel can safely perform.

The contract between a shipowner and a charterer setting out the terms on which a vessel is hired — by voyage, by time period, or by bareboat/demise. Charter party clauses govern everything from laytime and off-hire to performance warranties, and shape the commercial pressure under which vessels operate.

Estimating a vessel's current position from a known starting point using course steered, speed and elapsed time, without external position fixes. It remains a fundamental navigation skill and a sanity check on electronic systems — and in DP, the control system performs an analogous model-based estimate whenever position references drop out.

The total mass a ship can safely carry — cargo, fuel, fresh water, ballast, stores and crew — measured in tonnes. DWT describes carrying capacity, and should not be confused with gross tonnage, which measures internal volume.

The vertical distance from the waterline to the lowest point of a vessel's hull or appendages. Draught determines under-keel clearance, port access and loading condition, and is read from draught marks or sensors before critical passages.

terms.term: ECDIS — Electronic Chart Display and Information System
terms.def: The type-approved electronic navigation system that displays official electronic charts integrated with GNSS position, radar overlay and route monitoring, legally replacing paper charts when operated with approved backup. Generic and type-specific ECDIS training is mandatory for watchkeepers under STCW.

The vertical distance from the waterline to the freeboard deck, representing the vessel's reserve buoyancy. Minimum freeboard is fixed by the Load Line Convention and marked on the hull; loading beyond it is both unsafe and illegal.

terms.term: GMDSS — Global Maritime Distress and Safety System
terms.def: The internationally coordinated system of satellite and radio communications that ensures a vessel in distress can always alert rescue services and receive maritime safety information. GMDSS equipment carriage depends on the vessel's trading area, and officers hold dedicated GMDSS certificates to operate it.

A dimensionless index of a ship's total enclosed volume, calculated under the 1969 Tonnage Convention. GT drives a surprising amount of regulation — manning scales, survey regimes, port dues and which conventions apply — which is why "over 500 GT" appears so often in maritime rules.

One nautical mile per hour (1.852 km/h) — the standard unit of speed at sea and in aviation. The name survives from the days of measuring speed by counting knots in a log line paid out over a timed interval.

Any vessel or platform capable of drilling offshore wells and moving between locations — jack-ups, semi-submersibles and drillships. DP-operated MODUs (typically DP class 3) are among the most demanding station-keeping applications, since loss of position with a riser connected has severe consequences.

The family of vessels serving offshore energy operations: platform supply vessels, anchor handlers, subsea construction vessels, walk-to-work and service operation vessels for offshore wind, and more. Most modern OSVs are DP class 2, making the segment one of the largest employers of certified DPOs.

The documented berth-to-berth plan for a voyage, developed in four stages — appraisal, planning, execution and monitoring — covering routes, hazards, under-keel clearance, contingencies and reporting points. Passage planning is an STCW requirement and a recurring finding in both port state inspections and accident reports.

The conduct of a vessel through confined or hazardous waters with the assistance of a licensed local pilot, who advises the bridge team on local conditions while the master remains in command. Effective master–pilot exchange and bridge team integration are classic BRM topics.

An offshore vessel purpose-built to carry cargo — deck cargo, fuel, water, drilling fluids and dry bulk — between shore bases and offshore installations. PSVs routinely hold station on DP within the 500-metre safety zone of platforms, one of the highest-frequency close-proximity DP operations in the industry.

An unmanned, tethered underwater robot flown by pilots on the surface vessel, used for inspection, construction support and intervention. ROV operations from DP vessels create specific interface risks — umbilical management and vessel excursion limits — reflected in the ASOG for the task.

A specialised tanker that loads crude oil directly from offshore installations — via bow loading systems from FPSOs or offshore loading buoys — and shuttles it to shore terminals. Offshore loading is a precision DP operation, and shuttle tanker DPOs operate under some of the strictest competence and weather criteria in the industry.

The bodily sinkage and trim change a vessel experiences when moving through shallow water, caused by accelerated flow under the hull reducing pressure. Squat can significantly reduce under-keel clearance at speed and must be calculated in passage planning for shallow transits.

The vertical distance between the lowest point of the hull and the seabed. Company and port UKC policies define minimum clearances that must account for tide, squat, heel and swell — and verifying UKC along the whole route is a core element of passage planning.

The ship's "black box", continuously recording bridge audio, radar images, position, heading and key sensor data in a protected capsule. VDR data is invaluable in incident investigation, and replaying it has become a powerful tool for structured onboard debriefing and training.

A shore-based service that monitors and manages ship traffic in ports and congested waterways using radar, AIS and radio, providing information, traffic organisation and navigational assistance. Participation is mandatory in designated VTS areas, with reporting procedures set out in the sailing directions.
